title: Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff
summary: The container starts, exits, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with growing delay.

steps.title: Confirm it is actually looping
steps.look: RESTARTS climbing over successive checks. A high but static count is an old incident, not a live one.

signals.means: This is a Job or a one-shot container that finished. restartPolicy is wrong, not the app.

steps.title: Read the previous container's logs
steps.look: The FIRST fatal line, not the last. Startup errors scroll off the top and the tail is usually just the shutdown noise.

signals.means: It died waiting on a dependency that was not reachable.
Required configuration was absent at startup.
The process cannot read a path or bind a port as its runAsUser.

steps.title: Read the termination state
steps.look: exitCode and reason. This is the single most decisive field in the whole runbook.

signals.means: The kernel killed it for memory. No amount of restarting will fix this.
The entrypoint was found but is not executable. Check the file mode in the image.
The entrypoint was not found at all. Wrong path, or missing shell in a distroless base.
The application chose to exit. The reason is in the logs, not here.

steps.title: Check whether a probe is doing the killing
steps.look: Events for 'Liveness probe failed'. If present, the app may be healthy but slow to start, and the probe is executing it.

signals.means: The liveness probe is killing a container that may only need more startup time.

causes.cause: A required env var, Secret key or ConfigMap key is absent, so the process exits during startup.
causes.fix: Fix the owning Deployment/Secret/ConfigMap in source control and reconcile. Do not patch the live Pod.

causes.cause: The container's memory limit is below its real working set.
causes.fix: Raise limits.memory in the owning Deployment, or fix the leak. Restarting will reproduce it every time.

causes.cause: A database, cache or upstream service was not reachable at startup.
causes.fix: Confirm the dependency's Service has endpoints, then decide whether the app should retry instead of exiting.

causes.cause: initialDelaySeconds is shorter than the app's real startup time, so liveness kills it mid-boot.
causes.fix: Move the slow-start allowance to a startupProbe rather than inflating the liveness delay.

causes.cause: Exit 127. The command in the image manifest does not exist at that path.
causes.fix: Check the Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT/CMD against the built image. A distroless base has no /bin/sh.

causes.cause: Exit 126. The file exists but lacks the execute bit, or its interpreter line is wrong.
causes.fix: Add chmod +x in the Dockerfile, or fix the shebang. Rebuild the image.

causes.cause: runAsUser cannot read a mounted path or bind a privileged port.
causes.fix: Correct fsGroup on the volume, or move the app to a port above 1024.

causes.cause: A one-shot workload is running under restartPolicy Always.
causes.fix: Run it as a Job with restartPolicy OnFailure or Never.

verify: RESTARTS holds steady across at least three checks spanning the app's normal startup window.
The container reports Ready, and readiness has not flapped in recent events.
The original failing request or job path completes successfully.
escalate: Image tag and digest, plus resources and probe definitions

title: Pod stays Pending and is never scheduled
summary: The Pod object exists but no node has accepted it.

steps.title: Read the scheduler's own reason
steps.look: The scheduler states exactly why each node was rejected, in the form '0/N nodes are available: ...'. Read that string before anything else.

signals.means: No node has enough free allocatable resource for the requests.
The nodeSelector or affinity rule matches no node's labels.
Every candidate node carries a taint this Pod does not tolerate.
This is a storage problem wearing a scheduling costume.

signals.match: (?i)node\(s\) didn't find available persistent volumes|volume node affinity conflict
signals.means: The PV is pinned to a zone the scheduler cannot place the Pod in.

steps.title: Compare the request against real allocatable capacity
steps.look: Requests, not usage. A node at 12% CPU usage can still be 100% requested and therefore unschedulable.

steps.title: Read what this Pod is actually asking for
steps.look: Compare these three against the previous step. The mismatch is usually obvious once both are on screen.

causes.cause: The sum of requests exceeds allocatable on every node.
causes.fix: Lower the request to the workload's real profile, or add capacity. Raising the limit does not help; the scheduler reads requests.

causes.cause: nodeSelector or nodeAffinity references labels no node carries, often after a node pool was replaced.
causes.fix: Correct the selector, or label the intended nodes. Check for typos in the label key first.

causes.cause: Nodes are tainted (NoSchedule) and the Pod has no matching toleration.
causes.fix: Add the toleration if the Pod belongs on those nodes, otherwise target a different pool.

causes.cause: A referenced PVC has not bound, so the Pod cannot be placed.
causes.fix: Follow the PVC Pending runbook. Nothing about the Pod spec will fix this.

causes.cause: An existing PV lives in one zone and the Pod cannot be scheduled there.
causes.fix: Use a topology-aware StorageClass with volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer.

verify: The Pod reports a nodeName and moves past Pending.
No new FailedScheduling events appear for this Pod.
The change was made in the owning manifest, not by editing the live Pod.
escalate: Allocated resources block from describe nodes
The Pod's requests, nodeSelector and tolerations

title: Service exists but returns connection refused
summary: DNS resolves the Service, but nothing answers. Usually the Service has no endpoints.

steps.title: Check whether the Service has any endpoints at all
steps.look: ENDPOINTS column. If it is empty or <none>, the Service is pointing at nothing and the problem is the selector or pod readiness, not the network.

signals.means: No pods are backing this Service.

steps.title: Compare the Service selector against real pod labels
steps.cmd: kubectl get svc {service} -n {namespace} -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}{"\n"}' && kubectl get pods -n {namespace} --show-labels
steps.look: An exact match on every key. One extra or renamed label is enough to produce an empty Service, and this is the most common cause by a wide margin.

signals.means: Compare character by character. 'app' and 'app.kubernetes.io/name' are different keys.

steps.title: Check whether the backing pods are Ready
steps.look: A pod that is Running but 0/1 Ready is excluded from endpoints. Readiness, not liveness, controls Service membership.

signals.means: The pod is up but failing readiness, so it is deliberately kept out of the Service.

steps.title: Confirm the target port matches the container port
steps.look: targetPort must match the container's real listening port, or a named port the container declares. port is what clients dial; targetPort is where it lands.

causes.cause: The Service selector does not match the pod labels.
causes.fix: Align them in the manifests. Changing the Deployment's pod labels forces a rollout, so prefer correcting the Service.

causes.cause: Pods are running but failing their readiness probe, so kube-proxy excludes them.
causes.fix: Fix the readiness endpoint or its threshold. The Service will populate on its own once pods report Ready.

causes.cause: targetPort points at a port nothing is listening on.
causes.fix: Set targetPort to the container's real port, or use a named port so the two cannot drift.

verify: EndpointSlice lists the expected pod IPs.
A request from inside the cluster to the Service name succeeds.
The count of endpoints matches the number of Ready replicas.

title: ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull
summary: The kubelet cannot fetch the image. The event message says which of four reasons.

steps.title: Read the pull failure message
steps.look: The Failed event's message. It names the exact reason, and each reason has a different owner.

signals.means: The tag does not exist in the registry.
The node has no valid credentials for this registry.
TLS trust failure between the node and the registry.
The node could not reach the registry at all.

steps.title: Check the image reference on the pod
steps.look: Typos in the registry host or tag are the single most common cause. Read it character by character.

steps.title: Check whether a pull secret is attached
steps.look: Empty output on a private registry means the pod has no credentials. The secret must live in the same namespace as the pod.

causes.cause: The tag does not exist in the repository.
causes.fix: Fix the tag in the manifest. Prefer pinning by digest for anything production.

causes.cause: No imagePullSecret, or it exists in a different namespace.
causes.fix: Create the secret in this namespace and reference it on the pod or its ServiceAccount.

causes.cause: The node does not trust the registry's certificate.
causes.fix: Install the CA on the nodes. Do not mark the registry insecure.

causes.cause: The node has no network path to the registry.
causes.fix: Check egress rules, the NAT gateway and any proxy configuration on the nodes.

verify: The pod moves past ImagePullBackOff and the container starts.
No new Failed pull events appear.
escalate: Whether an imagePullSecret is attached and in which namespace

title: Container was OOMKilled
summary: The kernel killed the container for exceeding its memory limit. Restarting reproduces it.

steps.title: Confirm it was memory and not an external kill
steps.look: OOMKilled specifically. Exit 137 alone only means SIGKILL, which something else could have sent.

signals.means: The kernel's OOM killer took it. This is a limit problem, not a crash.

steps.title: Read the configured limit
steps.look: Compare limits.memory against what the process actually needs. If requests and limits differ widely, scheduling and eviction behave in ways you may not expect.

steps.title: Look at actual usage while it runs
steps.look: Usage climbing steadily towards the limit points at a leak. Usage spiking at a particular operation points at a batch size or a large request.

steps.title: Check whether the whole node is under pressure
steps.cmd: kubectl describe node $(kubectl get pod {pod} -n {namespace} -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}') | grep -A5 Conditions
steps.look: MemoryPressure true means the node is squeezed and eviction is in play, which is a different problem from a single container's limit.

causes.cause: The limit is below the real working set.
causes.fix: Raise limits.memory in the owning Deployment. Measure first with kubectl top rather than guessing.

causes.cause: Memory grows without bound until the limit is reached.
causes.fix: Raising the limit only delays it. Profile the application; the limit is doing its job.

causes.cause: A JVM or Node process sized its heap against the node rather than the cgroup.
causes.fix: Set an explicit max heap, or use a runtime version that is container-aware.

causes.cause: The node is out of memory and evicting pods.
causes.fix: Check requests across the node. Under-requesting causes overcommit and cascading evictions.

verify: RESTARTS holds steady through a full workload cycle.
kubectl top shows headroom between usage and the limit.
escalate: kubectl top output over a few minutes

title: Deployment rollout never finishes
summary: kubectl rollout status hangs. New pods are not becoming ready, or the old ones will not go.

steps.title: Read the rollout condition
steps.look: The Progressing condition's reason. ProgressDeadlineExceeded means it gave up; that reason names the layer at fault.

signals.means: The new ReplicaSet never became available in time.
Still in progress. Give it the deadline before treating it as stuck.

steps.title: Find what the new pods are doing
steps.look: The newest pods. Pending means scheduling, CrashLoop means the app, 0/1 Running means readiness.

signals.means: Scheduling, not deployment. Follow the Pending runbook.
The new image does not start. Follow the CrashLoop runbook.
The container runs but fails readiness.

steps.title: Check whether a disruption budget is blocking removal
steps.look: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS at zero means old pods cannot be evicted, so the rollout cannot proceed.

steps.title: Check the surge and unavailable settings
steps.look: maxSurge 0 with maxUnavailable 0 is a deadlock: nothing new can start and nothing old can stop.

causes.cause: The new image fails to start.
causes.fix: Roll back, then fix the image. kubectl rollout undo restores the previous ReplicaSet.

causes.cause: New pods run but never pass readiness.
causes.fix: Check the probe path, port and initial delay against the new image's real startup.

causes.cause: New pods cannot be placed.
causes.fix: Follow the Pending runbook. Often the surge replica has nowhere to go.

causes.cause: A PodDisruptionBudget forbids removing the old pods.
causes.fix: Relax minAvailable, or scale up so the budget can be satisfied during the roll.

causes.cause: maxSurge and maxUnavailable are both zero.
causes.fix: Set at least one of them above zero.

verify: kubectl rollout status returns successfully.
All replicas are on the new ReplicaSet and Ready.

title: Node is NotReady
summary: The node stopped reporting healthy. Pods on it will be evicted after the toleration window.

steps.title: Read the node's conditions
steps.look: Which condition is false or unknown. Ready Unknown means the kubelet stopped reporting entirely, which is very different from a pressure condition.

signals.means: The kubelet stopped posting status. The node may be gone or partitioned.
The node is out of disk.
The node is out of memory.
Process ID exhaustion, usually a fork loop.
The CNI has not configured the node's network.

steps.title: Check how long it has been unhealthy
steps.look: The age against the last transition. Pods are evicted after the not-ready toleration, five minutes by default.

steps.title: See what is still on it
steps.look: Anything not yet evicted. Stateful workloads here need attention before the node is replaced.

steps.title: Cordon it so nothing new lands
steps.look: The node shows SchedulingDisabled. Do this before investigating so the problem does not spread.
steps.note: Marks the node unschedulable. Running pods are not touched, but nothing new will be placed. Reverse with kubectl uncordon.

causes.cause: The kubelet is not posting status.
causes.fix: Check the host: is it up, is the kubelet service running, can it reach the API server.

causes.cause: The node's disk is full, often image or log growth.
causes.fix: Clear space, then set image garbage collection and log rotation so it does not recur.

causes.cause: The node is out of memory.
causes.fix: Look for pods without limits. Overcommit on requests is the usual root cause.

causes.cause: Process ID exhaustion.
causes.fix: Find the fork loop. Set a pid limit on the offending workload.

causes.cause: The CNI plugin has not initialised on the node.
causes.fix: Check the CNI DaemonSet's pod on that node.

verify: The node reports Ready.
Workloads have rescheduled and are serving.
The condition that flipped has a remediation, not just a restart.
escalate: Whether the host is reachable outside Kubernetes
Pods still bound to the node

title: PersistentVolumeClaim stays Pending
summary: The claim never binds, so every pod using it stays Pending too.

steps.title: Read the binding events
steps.look: The provisioner's own message. WaitForFirstConsumer is not an error at all; it is the expected state until a pod is scheduled.

signals.means: Normal. The volume binds when a pod that uses it gets scheduled.
The named StorageClass does not exist in this cluster.
Static provisioning with no matching PV.
The provisioner tried and the backend refused.

steps.title: Check the requested class and access mode
steps.look: ReadWriteMany is unsupported by most block storage drivers and is a common silent mismatch.

steps.title: List the classes that actually exist
steps.look: Whether the requested name exists, and which class is marked default. An empty storageClassName uses the default; a missing default leaves the claim Pending forever.

causes.cause: The class uses WaitForFirstConsumer.
causes.fix: Nothing is wrong. Schedule a pod that mounts it and it will bind.

causes.cause: The named class does not exist.
causes.fix: Correct the name, or install the class. Cluster migrations often leave stale names in manifests.

causes.cause: Static provisioning with no PV matching size, class and access mode.
causes.fix: Create a matching PV, or move to dynamic provisioning.

causes.cause: The driver does not support the requested access mode.
causes.fix: Use ReadWriteOnce for block storage, or a filesystem driver for ReadWriteMany.

causes.cause: The storage backend rejected the request, often on quota.
causes.fix: Read the provisioner's message and check the cloud-side quota.

verify: The PVC reports Bound with a volume name.
The pod that needed it is scheduled and running.
escalate: Requested class, size and access mode

title: DNS resolution fails inside pods
summary: Names do not resolve from within the cluster. Work out whether it is CoreDNS, the pod's resolver, or upstream.

steps.title: Test resolution of a cluster name from the pod
steps.look: An IP means cluster DNS works and the problem is narrower than you thought. Nothing means the resolver path is broken.

signals.means: Cluster DNS works. Test an external name next.
Cluster DNS is not answering for this pod.

steps.title: Check that CoreDNS is running
steps.cmd: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide
steps.look: All replicas Ready. CrashLooping CoreDNS is usually a bad Corefile edit or a resolver loop.

signals.means: CoreDNS itself is failing. Check its logs for a loop plugin detection.
CoreDNS is not ready, so nothing in the cluster resolves.

steps.title: Read the pod's resolver configuration
steps.look: The nameserver should be the cluster DNS Service IP. A node-level resolver here means dnsPolicy is wrong for a cluster workload.

signals.means: Normal, but it means short names try several search domains first, which looks like slow DNS under load.
The pod is using a node or public resolver, not cluster DNS.

steps.title: Test an external name
steps.look: Cluster names working but external failing points at CoreDNS's upstream forwarder or egress, not at Kubernetes DNS itself.

causes.cause: CoreDNS is unhealthy.
causes.fix: Read its logs. A loop plugin error means the upstream resolver points back at CoreDNS.

causes.cause: The pod uses host DNS instead of cluster DNS.
causes.fix: Set dnsPolicy ClusterFirst. hostNetwork pods need ClusterFirstWithHostNet explicitly.

causes.cause: CoreDNS cannot reach its upstream resolver.
causes.fix: Check the forward directive in the Corefile and egress from the CoreDNS pods.

causes.cause: Short names expand through five search domains before the real lookup.
causes.fix: Use fully qualified names with a trailing dot for hot paths, or tune ndots per pod.

causes.cause: A NetworkPolicy blocks egress to port 53.
causes.fix: Allow UDP and TCP 53 to kube-system in the policy.

verify: Both cluster and external names resolve from inside the pod.
CoreDNS replicas are Ready with no restarts.
escalate: Which names fail: cluster, external, or both

title: Ingress returns 502, 503 or 404
summary: The ingress answers but the backend does not. Each status points at a different layer.

steps.title: Identify which status you get and from whom
steps.look: The Server header tells you whether the ingress controller answered or something upstream did. 404 usually means no rule matched; 503 usually means no healthy backend.

signals.means: The controller matched a rule but has no healthy endpoint behind it.
No ingress rule matched this host and path.
The controller reached a backend and got an invalid response.

steps.title: Check the ingress has an address and correct rules
steps.look: An empty ADDRESS means no controller has claimed it, usually a missing or wrong ingressClassName.

steps.title: Check the backend service has endpoints
steps.look: Empty endpoints produce 503 every time. This is the most common cause by a wide margin.

signals.means: No pods behind the service. Follow the no-endpoints runbook.

steps.title: Read the controller's own logs
steps.look: The controller logs the upstream it chose and why it failed. This is more precise than anything you can infer from the client side.

causes.cause: The backend service has no ready endpoints.
causes.fix: Fix pod readiness or the service selector. The ingress is working correctly by refusing to send traffic nowhere.

causes.cause: Host or path in the request does not match any rule.
causes.fix: Check pathType. Prefix and Exact behave differently, and this catches people out constantly.

causes.cause: No controller claimed the ingress.
causes.fix: Set ingressClassName to a class that exists in the cluster.

causes.cause: The backend returned something the controller could not use.
causes.fix: Check the app's own logs. Often TLS expected on a plain-HTTP backend port.

causes.cause: The ingress points at a service port that does not exist.
causes.fix: Match the port name or number to the service definition.

verify: The URL returns the expected status from the application.
The controller logs show the correct upstream being selected.
escalate: The exact status and response headers
Controller log lines for the request

title: Pods are being Evicted
summary: The kubelet is reclaiming resources on a node under pressure. The eviction message names which resource.
aliases: the node was low on resource

steps.title: List the evicted pods and read the reason
steps.look: The message names the resource that ran out. That single word decides everything that follows.

signals.means: The pod wrote too much to its writable layer or an emptyDir.
The node ran out of memory and reclaimed the largest offender over its request.
The node exhausted inodes, usually many small files.

steps.title: Find which node is under pressure
steps.look: Which nodes report DiskPressure or MemoryPressure. If it is one node, it is a host problem; if it is all of them, it is a capacity problem.

steps.title: Check whether the evicted workload declared requests
steps.cmd: kubectl get pod {pod} -n {namespace} -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources.requests}' 2>/dev/null || echo 'pod already removed'
steps.look: Pods without requests are evicted first. Declaring a request is what buys a workload protection.

causes.cause: The container wrote more to local disk than its ephemeral-storage allowance.
causes.fix: Set an ephemeral-storage request and limit, and move logs to stdout rather than files.

causes.cause: The node ran out of memory.
causes.fix: Set memory requests on the workloads sharing that node. Eviction targets pods exceeding their request first.

causes.cause: Inode exhaustion from many small files.
causes.fix: Find the directory generating them. Log rotation usually solves it.

causes.cause: Best-effort pods are evicted first.
causes.fix: Declare requests so the workload gets a guaranteed or burstable class.

verify: No new evictions during a normal workload window.
The node's pressure conditions are false.
The affected workloads declare requests.
escalate: Whether the workload declares requests and limits

title: Forbidden: User cannot perform this action
summary: The API server authenticated you but refused the operation. The message names exactly what is missing.

steps.title: Read the forbidden message in full
steps.look: The message names the identity, the verb, the resource and the namespace. All four matter and the fix depends on which one is wrong.

signals.means: A ServiceAccount, not you. Something is running with in-cluster credentials.
The resource is cluster-scoped, so a namespaced Role cannot grant it.
Namespaced. A RoleBinding in that namespace will do it.

steps.title: Ask the API server directly whether you can do it
steps.look: A definitive yes or no from the authorizer itself, with no guessing about which binding applies.

steps.title: List everything your identity can do here
steps.look: The full effective permission set. Comparing this against what you expected usually makes the gap obvious.

steps.title: Find which bindings mention your identity
steps.look: Which roles are actually attached. An empty result means nothing grants you anything in this namespace.

causes.cause: No Role or RoleBinding grants this verb in this namespace.
causes.fix: Create a RoleBinding to a Role carrying that verb. Grant the narrowest set that works.

causes.cause: The resource is cluster-scoped.
causes.fix: A ClusterRoleBinding is required. A namespaced RoleBinding cannot grant cluster-scoped access however it is written.

causes.cause: The request is from a ServiceAccount, not your user.
causes.fix: Bind the role to that ServiceAccount. Pods use their SA, never your kubeconfig.

causes.cause: You are authenticated as a different identity than you assumed.
causes.fix: Check kubectl config current-context. Multi-cluster setups make this a routine mistake.

causes.cause: A ClusterRole relies on aggregation labels that do not match.
causes.fix: Check the aggregationRule selectors against the labels on the contributing roles.

verify: kubectl auth can-i returns yes.
The operation succeeds.
The grant is as narrow as the task requires.

title: HorizontalPodAutoscaler is not scaling
summary: Load is high but replica count does not move. Usually metrics, not the policy.

steps.title: Read the HPA's current targets
steps.look: The TARGETS column. <unknown> means no metrics are arriving and the HPA is inert; a real percentage means metrics work and the policy is the question.

signals.means: No metrics. The HPA cannot make any decision at all.
Metrics are flowing. Read the conditions for why it is holding.

steps.title: Read the scaling conditions
steps.look: ScalingLimited with a reason names the exact constraint, such as having hit maxReplicas or being inside the stabilisation window.

signals.means: Already at maxReplicas. The ceiling is the constraint.
metrics-server is not returning usage for these pods.
It is deliberately holding, usually the stabilisation window.

steps.title: Check metrics-server is healthy
steps.look: If this errors, the HPA has the same problem. metrics-server is the dependency for all resource-based autoscaling.

steps.title: Check the pods declare requests
steps.look: CPU utilisation is a percentage of the request. With no request declared there is no denominator, so the HPA can never compute a target.

causes.cause: metrics-server is absent or not serving.
causes.fix: Install or repair it. Check its pod logs for TLS errors against the kubelet, which is the usual failure.

causes.cause: Containers declare no CPU request.
causes.fix: Set one. Utilisation is meaningless without it and the HPA will show unknown forever.

causes.cause: Already at maxReplicas.
causes.fix: Raise maxReplicas if capacity allows. Confirm nodes can actually take more pods first.

causes.cause: The scale-down stabilisation window is holding it.
causes.fix: Expected behaviour preventing flapping. Tune behaviour.scaleDown if genuinely too slow.

causes.cause: scaleTargetRef points at something that does not exist.
causes.fix: Check the name and kind match the real workload exactly.

verify: TARGETS shows real percentages.
Replicas move under load and settle after.
Pods have requests declared.

title: ConfigMap or Secret change is not picked up
summary: You updated the config but the application still uses the old values.

steps.title: Confirm the ConfigMap itself actually changed
steps.look: The values as stored. If they are old here, the apply never landed and nothing downstream matters.

steps.title: Check how the pod consumes it
steps.look: envFrom and env never update in a running container, ever. Volume mounts do update, but on the kubelet's sync period rather than instantly.

signals.means: Consumed as environment variables. These are fixed at container start and will never refresh.
Mounted as a volume. It refreshes, but not immediately.

steps.title: Check when the pod started relative to the change
steps.look: A pod older than the ConfigMap edit is still holding whatever existed at its start.

steps.title: Restart the workload to pick up the new values
steps.look: New pods with fresh timestamps. Watch rollout status rather than assuming it worked.
steps.note: Replaces every pod in the deployment with a rolling update. Brief capacity reduction during the roll, and if the new config is wrong the new pods will fail. Confirm the ConfigMap contents are correct before restarting rather than after.

causes.cause: Consumed as environment variables, which are set once at container start.
causes.fix: Restart the workload. To make this automatic, hash the config into a pod annotation so any change triggers a roll.

causes.cause: Mounted as a volume, which refreshes on the kubelet sync period.
causes.fix: Wait about a minute, or restart. subPath mounts never refresh at all, which surprises people.

causes.cause: Mounted with subPath.
causes.fix: subPath mounts are a point-in-time copy and do not update. Mount the directory instead.

causes.cause: The change never reached the cluster.
causes.fix: Check you applied to the right namespace and context.

causes.cause: The application read the config once at startup.
causes.fix: Restarting is the only option unless the app watches the file itself.

verify: The running pod shows the new values.
The application behaves according to the new config.
The mechanism for future updates is understood.
escalate: Pod start time versus the change time

title: StatefulSet will not progress past a pod
summary: Ordered rollout blocks on one replica and nothing after it starts.

steps.title: See which ordinal is blocking
steps.look: StatefulSets proceed strictly in order. The lowest-numbered unhealthy pod is the only one that matters; everything above it is simply waiting.

signals.means: The blocking pod cannot be scheduled, very often because its PVC has not bound.
The blocking pod starts and dies.

steps.title: Check its volume claim
steps.look: Each ordinal gets its own PVC. A single unbound claim halts the whole set, and this is the most common cause.

steps.title: Read the update strategy
steps.look: OnDelete means the controller will never replace pods by itself and you must delete them manually. A partition value means updates deliberately stop at that ordinal.

steps.title: Check whether pod management is the constraint
steps.look: OrderedReady is the default and enforces the strict sequence. Parallel lets pods start independently, which suits some workloads and not others.

causes.cause: The blocking pod's PVC has not bound.
causes.fix: Follow the PVC Pending runbook. The StatefulSet is behaving correctly by waiting.

causes.cause: The application in that ordinal fails to start.
causes.fix: Treat it as a CrashLoop. Often ordinal zero is a cluster seed and its failure is different from the others.

causes.cause: updateStrategy is OnDelete.
causes.fix: Delete the pods yourself in order. The controller will not do it.

causes.cause: A partition is set on the rolling update.
causes.fix: Lower the partition value to allow more ordinals to update.

causes.cause: A clustered application cannot reach quorum.
causes.fix: Check the app's own cluster state. Kubernetes sees healthy processes that refuse to serve.

verify: All ordinals are Running and Ready in sequence.
Each has a bound PVC.
The application reports a healthy cluster.
escalate: Update strategy and pod management policy

title: Traffic blocked between pods after a NetworkPolicy
summary: Connections that used to work now time out. Policies are deny-by-default once any policy selects a pod.

steps.title: List policies affecting this namespace
steps.look: Any policy at all changes the model for the pods it selects. Before the first policy everything is allowed; after it, only what is explicitly permitted.

signals.means: A default-deny policy exists. Every allowed flow must now be stated explicitly.

steps.title: Find which policies select this pod
steps.look: The podSelector on each policy against your pod's labels. A policy with an empty podSelector selects every pod in the namespace.

steps.title: Check the pod's own labels
steps.look: Whether the pod is selected by a policy and whether it matches any allow rule's peer selector. Both directions must permit the flow.

steps.title: Verify whether DNS is also blocked
steps.look: Egress policies frequently forget port 53, which makes everything look like a DNS outage when it is actually the policy.

signals.means: DNS is blocked too. The egress policy is missing a rule for port 53.

causes.cause: A default-deny policy applies and no rule permits this flow.
causes.fix: Add an explicit allow for it. Policies are additive, so a new permissive policy is safer than editing the deny.

causes.cause: Egress policy omits DNS.
causes.fix: Allow UDP and TCP 53 to kube-system. Almost every egress policy needs this and almost every first attempt forgets it.

causes.cause: Egress is allowed on the client but ingress is not allowed on the server.
causes.fix: Both ends must permit the flow. Check the policies selecting each side.

causes.cause: namespaceSelector matches on labels the target namespace does not carry.
causes.fix: Label the namespace. Namespaces have no useful labels by default.

causes.cause: The CNI plugin does not enforce NetworkPolicy.
causes.fix: Flannel ignores them entirely, so policies appear to apply and do nothing. Confirm your CNI supports them.

verify: The intended connection succeeds.
DNS still resolves from inside the pod.
Unintended flows remain blocked.
escalate: Whether DNS works from the client pod

title: Pod stuck in Init or PodInitializing
summary: An init container has not completed, so the main container never starts.

steps.title: See which init container is blocking
steps.look: Init containers run strictly in order. Only the first incomplete one matters; everything after it has not started.

signals.means: The init container runs and fails repeatedly.
It is still running, not failed. It may be waiting on something.

steps.title: Read that init container's logs
steps.look: Init containers are frequently wait loops for a database or a migration. The log usually says exactly what it is waiting for.

steps.title: Check what it is waiting on is actually reachable
steps.look: A wait-for-dependency init container blocks forever if the dependency never becomes ready, which looks like the pod being stuck.

steps.title: Check init containers have their own resources
steps.look: Init containers are scheduled with the pod. An init container requesting more than the node has keeps the whole pod Pending.

causes.cause: The init container exits non-zero.
causes.fix: Read its logs. The pod will never start until it exits zero.

causes.cause: It is waiting on an unavailable dependency.
causes.fix: Make the dependency ready. Add a timeout so it fails loudly rather than hanging forever.

causes.cause: A database migration init container is blocked on a lock.
causes.fix: Find the holder. Concurrent replicas running the same migration cause this.

causes.cause: Init containers are in the wrong order.
causes.fix: They run sequentially in declaration order. Reorder them.

verify: The pod moves past Init and the main container starts.
Init containers complete in a few seconds, not minutes.
escalate: Logs from the blocking init container

title: Job or CronJob never completes
summary: The Job stays active, retries forever, or the CronJob never fires at all.

steps.title: Read the Job's status
steps.look: Active, succeeded and failed counts with any condition. BackoffLimitExceeded means it gave up after repeated failures.

signals.means: It retried up to the limit and failed every time.
It exceeded activeDeadlineSeconds and was killed.

steps.title: Read logs from the failed pods
steps.look: The actual failure. Job pods are retained after failure specifically so you can read this.

steps.title: For a CronJob, check schedule and last run
steps.look: suspend true means it will never fire. The schedule is evaluated in the controller's timezone, which is UTC unless configured otherwise.

signals.means: The CronJob is suspended.

steps.title: Check for concurrency blocking a new run
steps.look: With concurrencyPolicy Forbid, a run still active blocks the next one. A hung job silently stops all future runs.

causes.cause: The job's pod fails every attempt.
causes.fix: Fix the command. Raise backoffLimit only once the failure is understood.

causes.cause: activeDeadlineSeconds was exceeded.
causes.fix: Raise it, or make the job faster. The deadline counts total time, not per attempt.

causes.cause: The CronJob is suspended.
causes.fix: Set suspend to false. Often left on after an incident and forgotten.

causes.cause: The schedule is in UTC, not local time.
causes.fix: Set spec.timeZone, or express the schedule in UTC deliberately.

causes.cause: A previous run is still active.
causes.fix: Find and clear it. Consider Replace rather than Forbid.

causes.cause: restartPolicy is not Never or OnFailure.
causes.fix: Job pods must use one of those two. Always is rejected.

verify: The Job reports succeeded.
A CronJob fires on schedule.
Failed runs are visible rather than silent.
escalate: CronJob schedule, suspend flag and last schedule time

title: Pod stuck Terminating forever
summary: Deletion was requested but the pod never goes. Usually a finalizer or an unresponsive node.

steps.title: Check for finalizers and the grace period
steps.look: A finalizer means something must run before deletion completes. A long grace period means it may simply need more time.

signals.means: A finalizer is present and its controller has not released it.
The grace period is very long. It may be working as configured.

steps.title: Check whether the node is healthy
steps.cmd: kubectl get pod {pod} -n {namespace} -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}' && kubectl get nodes
steps.look: If the node is NotReady, the kubelet cannot confirm deletion. Pods on a dead node stay Terminating indefinitely by design.

signals.means: The node is unreachable, so deletion can never be confirmed.

steps.title: Check whether the process ignores SIGTERM
steps.look: A process ignoring SIGTERM runs until the grace period expires and is then SIGKILLed. That is slow but not stuck.

steps.title: Remove the finalizer to force deletion
steps.look: The pod disappears. Check for orphaned resources on the cloud side afterwards.
steps.note: Removes the finalizer without letting its controller do the cleanup it was waiting to perform. That cleanup may include detaching a volume or deregistering from a load balancer, and skipping it can leave orphaned cloud resources or a volume that cannot attach elsewhere. Understand which controller owns the finalizer before doing this.

causes.cause: A controller's finalizer has not been released.
causes.fix: Find that controller and fix it. Removing the finalizer skips its cleanup.

causes.cause: The node is unreachable.
causes.fix: The pod clears when the node returns, or when it is deleted from the cluster. Force deletion risks two copies running.

causes.cause: The grace period is genuinely long.
causes.fix: Wait. Or shorten terminationGracePeriodSeconds if the value is not justified.

causes.cause: The process does not handle SIGTERM.
causes.fix: Handle it in the application. PID 1 in a container does not get default signal handling.

causes.cause: A volume cannot detach.
causes.fix: Check the CSI driver. This is common with cloud block storage under load.

verify: The pod is gone.
No orphaned volume or load balancer registration remains.
The root cause was addressed, not just forced past.

title: Cannot create pods: exceeded quota
summary: The namespace has hit a ResourceQuota, so new workloads are refused at admission.

steps.title: Read the quota and current usage
steps.look: Used against Hard for each resource. The one at its limit is named in the rejection message.

signals.means: A compute quota is exhausted.
The pod count limit is reached.
The PVC count limit is reached.

steps.title: Check whether a LimitRange forces defaults
steps.look: A LimitRange injects default requests into pods that declare none. Those defaults count against the quota and are often larger than expected.

steps.title: Find what is consuming the quota
steps.look: Requests per pod. Completed Job pods still count until they are cleaned up, which surprises people.

steps.title: Clear completed pods holding quota
steps.look: The quota's Used figure drops. Recheck with describe resourcequota.
steps.note: Deletes every succeeded pod in the namespace, which also removes their logs. If anyone needs those logs for an audit or a debugging session, collect them first. Running pods are not affected.

causes.cause: CPU or memory requests are exhausted.
causes.fix: Raise the quota, or lower requests on existing workloads. Requests count, not usage.

causes.cause: The pod count limit is reached.
causes.fix: Clean up completed pods, or raise the limit.

causes.cause: The PVC count or storage limit is reached.
causes.fix: Remove unused claims, or raise the quota.

causes.cause: LimitRange defaults are larger than the workload needs.
causes.fix: Declare explicit requests so the default does not apply.

causes.cause: The quota requires requests and the pod declares none.
causes.fix: With a compute quota, every pod must declare requests. Add them or add a LimitRange.

verify: New pods are admitted.
Used sits comfortably below Hard.
Requests reflect real needs rather than defaults.

title: kubectl cannot reach the cluster
summary: Connection refused or timeout before any authentication happens.
aliases: unable to connect to the server

steps.title: Read the exact connection error
steps.look: Refused, timeout and no-such-host are three different problems. The wording tells you which.

signals.means: DNS cannot resolve the API server name.
Reached the host, nothing listening on the port.
No response at all, usually a firewall or missing VPN.
TLS problem with the cluster certificate.

steps.title: Check which context is active
steps.cmd: kubectl config current-context && kubectl config view --minify
steps.look: The server URL in use. A stale context pointing at a deleted cluster produces exactly this and is very common with multiple clusters.

steps.title: Test the endpoint directly
steps.look: A 401 or 403 is good news: the server is reachable and the problem is credentials. No response at all is network.

steps.title: Check the VPN or bastion requirement
steps.look: Private clusters are only reachable over VPN or through a bastion. This is the most common cause of a sudden timeout that worked yesterday.

causes.cause: The API server name does not resolve.
causes.fix: Check the URL in the kubeconfig. Private clusters often resolve only over VPN.

causes.cause: Nothing is listening on that port.
causes.fix: Check the cluster exists and the endpoint is right. A deleted cluster leaves a working kubeconfig.

causes.cause: Traffic is blocked.
causes.fix: Connect the VPN, or add your IP to the authorised networks list.

causes.cause: TLS verification fails against the cluster certificate.
causes.fix: Refresh the kubeconfig from the provider. Certificates rotate.

causes.cause: The credential expired.
causes.fix: Re-authenticate. Cloud kubeconfigs use short-lived tokens fetched by an exec plugin.

causes.cause: The active context points elsewhere.
causes.fix: kubectl config use-context with the right name.

verify: kubectl get nodes returns.
The active context is the intended cluster.
It works from a fresh shell.
escalate: Whether the endpoint responds to curl

title: Readiness or liveness probe keeps failing
summary: The container runs but the probe says otherwise, so it is removed from service or restarted.

steps.title: Read the probe failure events
steps.look: Which probe and what it reported. Liveness failures restart the container; readiness failures only remove it from endpoints.

signals.means: Nothing is listening on the probe port.
The probe path does not exist.
The endpoint exists and reports an error.
The endpoint is too slow for timeoutSeconds.

steps.title: Read the probe configuration
steps.look: Path, port, initialDelaySeconds, timeoutSeconds and thresholds. A timeout of one second against an endpoint that touches a database is a recipe for flapping.

steps.title: Call the probe endpoint from inside the pod
steps.look: What the kubelet would see. Working here but failing as a probe usually means the port or path in the spec is wrong.

steps.title: Check whether it needs a startup probe instead
steps.look: A slow-starting app killed by liveness during boot should use a startupProbe. Inflating the liveness delay to compensate weakens it for the whole lifetime.

causes.cause: Nothing listens on the probe port.
causes.fix: Check the port matches and the app binds 0.0.0.0 rather than localhost.

causes.cause: The probe path returns 404.
causes.fix: Point it at a real endpoint. A trailing slash can matter.

causes.cause: The endpoint reports an error.
causes.fix: The probe is correct. Fix the application.

causes.cause: The endpoint is slower than timeoutSeconds.
causes.fix: Raise the timeout, or make the health check lightweight. It should not query the database.

causes.cause: The app needs longer to boot than initialDelaySeconds.
causes.fix: Use a startupProbe. That is exactly what it exists for.

causes.cause: Liveness restarts a container that is merely busy.
causes.fix: Liveness should detect deadlock, not load. Most services need only readiness.

verify: The container reports Ready and stays Ready.
No probe failure events during normal load.
Liveness is not restarting a healthy container.
escalate: Result of calling the endpoint from inside the pod

title: Volume bound but pod cannot mount it
summary: The PVC is Bound yet the pod fails with a mount or attach error.

steps.title: Read the mount failure event
steps.look: The message names the volume and the reason. Multi-Attach, timeout and permission are three different fixes.

signals.means: The volume is still attached to another node.
The attach never completed, usually a CSI driver problem.
Mounted, but the container's user cannot write to it.

steps.title: Find where the volume is currently attached
steps.look: Which node holds it. A ReadWriteOnce volume can only attach to one node at a time, which is the cause of every Multi-Attach error.

steps.title: Check the CSI driver pods are healthy
steps.cmd: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | findstr csi
steps.look: The driver's node plugin must be running on the target node. A crashed node plugin makes every mount on that node hang.

steps.title: Check the access mode against the workload
steps.look: ReadWriteOnce with a multi-replica Deployment is a guaranteed Multi-Attach failure during any rolling update.

causes.cause: A ReadWriteOnce volume is attached elsewhere.
causes.fix: Ensure the old pod is fully gone. Use Recreate rather than RollingUpdate for single-writer volumes.

causes.cause: The CSI driver cannot complete the attach.
causes.fix: Check the driver's node plugin logs on the target node.

causes.cause: The container user cannot write to the mount.
causes.fix: Set fsGroup in the pod security context so the volume is chowned on mount.

causes.cause: The node has reached its volume attachment limit.
causes.fix: Cloud providers cap attachments per instance. Spread the pods or use larger nodes.

causes.cause: The volume is in a different zone than the node.
causes.fix: Use a topology-aware StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer.

verify: The pod mounts and starts.
No FailedMount events remain.
The access mode matches how the workload actually runs.
escalate: Which node holds the volume attachment
CSI driver pod status on the target node

title: kubectl logs returns nothing or the wrong thing
summary: You cannot see the output you need, so you are debugging blind.

steps.title: List every container in the pod
steps.look: A multi-container pod requires -c. Without it kubectl picks the first container, which in a service mesh is often the sidecar rather than your app.

signals.means: A service mesh sidecar is present. The default container may be the proxy.

steps.title: Read the previous instance for a restarting container
steps.look: For a crash loop, the current container has barely started. The previous one holds the failure.

steps.title: Check the container has started at all
steps.look: A container in Waiting has produced no logs because it has not run. That is not a logging problem.

steps.title: Check for a log rotation or collector taking them
steps.look: Timestamps reveal whether output is recent. The kubelet rotates container logs and only the current file is available through kubectl.

causes.cause: The pod has several containers.
causes.fix: Use -c with the container name. --all-containers works for a quick look.

causes.cause: The default container is a mesh sidecar.
causes.fix: Name your app container explicitly, or set the default-container annotation on the pod.

causes.cause: The container has not run.
causes.fix: Nothing to read. Follow the Init or CrashLoop runbook.

causes.cause: The kubelet rotated the log file.
causes.fix: Only the current file is available. Ship logs to a collector if you need history.

causes.cause: The app writes to a file inside the container.
causes.fix: Only stdout and stderr reach kubectl logs. Reconfigure the app.

verify: You can read the output you need.
For a crash loop you have the previous container's logs.
The right container is being read.
escalate: Whether the app logs to stdout

title: Pod fails because a Secret or ConfigMap is missing
summary: The pod cannot start because a referenced Secret or ConfigMap does not exist in this namespace.

steps.title: Read the config error
steps.look: CreateContainerConfigError names the exact object and key. This is the whole answer most of the time.

signals.means: The Secret does not exist in this namespace.
The ConfigMap does not exist in this namespace.
The object exists but the specific key does not.

steps.title: Check the object exists here
steps.look: Secrets and ConfigMaps are namespaced. An object in another namespace is invisible, which is the most common cause after a copy-paste between environments.

steps.title: Check the key name inside it
steps.look: The key names, not the values. Key names are case-sensitive and a hyphen against an underscore is enough to fail.

steps.title: Check what the pod is asking for
steps.look: Compare the requested names against what exists. Marking a reference optional lets the pod start without it, which may or may not be what you want.

causes.cause: The Secret or ConfigMap does not exist in this namespace.
causes.fix: Create it here. Objects do not cross namespaces.

causes.cause: The object exists but lacks the key.
causes.fix: Check spelling and case. Base64 encoding hides typos in values but not in key names.

causes.cause: It exists in a different namespace.
causes.fix: Copy it, or use an operator that replicates it deliberately.

causes.cause: The reference is required and absent.
causes.fix: Either create the object or mark the reference optional if the app can run without it.

causes.cause: A GitOps prune removed it.
causes.fix: Ensure it is managed in Git, or excluded from pruning if managed elsewhere.

verify: The pod starts.
The environment inside the container has the expected values.

title: Pod cannot schedule due to a host port conflict
summary: Only one pod per node can bind a given hostPort, so replicas collide.

steps.title: Read the scheduling reason
steps.look: A message about free ports means hostPort, not resources. That distinction saves a lot of wasted investigation.

signals.means: A hostPort is already taken on every candidate node.
A selector is also narrowing the candidates.

steps.title: Check whether the pod declares a hostPort
steps.look: hostPort binds the node's own port. Replicas exceeding the node count can never all be placed.

steps.title: Find what already holds it
steps.cmd: kubectl get pods -A -o wide | findstr /R "[0-9]" && kubectl get ds -A
steps.look: Every pod using a hostPort cluster-wide. Usually a DaemonSet already occupies it.

steps.title: Count schedulable nodes
steps.look: Replicas using hostPort cannot exceed the node count. That is a hard ceiling.

causes.cause: Another pod holds that host port on every node.
causes.fix: Drop hostPort and use a Service. hostPort is rarely the right tool outside DaemonSets.

causes.cause: More replicas than nodes.
causes.fix: hostPort caps replicas at one per node.

causes.cause: Selectors narrow the candidate nodes further.
causes.fix: Widen the selector or add nodes.

causes.cause: A DaemonSet already binds the port.
causes.fix: Pick a different port, or reconsider the design.

verify: The pod is scheduled.
The chosen approach scales past one pod per node.

title: kubectl exec fails
summary: You cannot get a shell in a running pod.

steps.title: Read the exec failure
steps.look: The wording separates a missing shell from a permissions problem from a connection problem.

signals.means: The image has no shell. Distroless and scratch images contain nothing but the binary.
The API server cannot reach the kubelet.
RBAC does not permit exec on pods.
The pod has several containers and none was named.

steps.title: Check the pod is actually running
steps.look: You cannot exec into a pod that is not Running. Terminating or Pending pods have no process to attach to.

steps.title: Try other shells the image might have
steps.look: Alpine has sh but not bash. Some images have neither, which is a deliberate hardening choice.

steps.title: Attach a debug container instead
steps.look: A shell with the target container's namespaces. The original container is untouched.
steps.note: Adds an ephemeral container to the running pod. The pod is not restarted and the application keeps serving, but the container persists for the pod's lifetime and shares its namespaces, so it can see the application's processes and network. On a cluster with admission policies this may be blocked or audited.

causes.cause: The image contains no shell.
causes.fix: Use kubectl debug with an ephemeral container. Do not add a shell to a hardened image just for debugging.

causes.cause: The pod has several containers.
causes.fix: Name one with -c.

causes.cause: You lack pods/exec permission.
causes.fix: Grant it. exec is a separate RBAC subresource from get.

causes.cause: The API server cannot reach the kubelet.
causes.fix: A node or network problem. Check node status.

causes.cause: The pod is not in Running state.
causes.fix: There is no process to attach to yet.

verify: You get a shell, or a debug container attached.
The original container was not modified.
escalate: Whether the image has a shell

title: Service endpoints keep appearing and disappearing
summary: Intermittent 502s because pods flap in and out of the Service.

steps.title: Watch the endpoints change
steps.look: Whether addresses come and go. A stable list means the problem is elsewhere; a changing one confirms flapping.

steps.title: Check readiness transitions on the pods
steps.look: Repeated Unhealthy events mean the readiness probe is failing intermittently, which is the usual cause.

signals.means: Readiness is flapping, so pods leave and rejoin the Service.

steps.title: Check whether restarts are occurring
steps.look: Climbing RESTARTS means liveness is killing containers, which is a stronger problem than readiness flapping.

steps.title: Check resource pressure on the pods
steps.look: CPU at the limit causes throttling, which makes probes time out. That is the most common hidden cause of flapping.

causes.cause: Readiness fails intermittently.
causes.fix: Raise timeoutSeconds and failureThreshold. The probe should not be as slow as a real request.

causes.cause: CPU limits cause throttling under load.
causes.fix: Raise the limit. A throttled container fails probes even though it is healthy.

causes.cause: The readiness endpoint does real work.
causes.fix: Make it cheap. It should not query the database on every probe.

causes.cause: Garbage collection pauses exceed the probe timeout.
causes.fix: Tune the heap, or raise the timeout above the worst pause.

causes.cause: Liveness is restarting containers.
causes.fix: Most services need only readiness. Liveness should detect deadlock, not slowness.

verify: The endpoint list is stable over several minutes.
No Unhealthy events during normal load.
Error rate returns to baseline.

title: Namespace stuck Terminating
summary: Deleting a namespace hangs forever because something in it will not finalize.

steps.title: Read the namespace conditions
steps.look: The conditions name which resources cannot be removed. This is far more useful than the Terminating status alone.

signals.means: Resources inside still exist and cannot be deleted.
An API service backing a custom resource is unavailable.

steps.title: Find what is still in it
steps.cmd: kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | ForEach-Object { kubectl get $_ -n {namespace} --ignore-not-found }
steps.look: Everything remaining. Custom resources with finalizers are the usual blocker.

steps.title: Check for unavailable API services
steps.look: A broken aggregated API server blocks namespace deletion entirely, because Kubernetes cannot enumerate its resources.

steps.title: Remove the finalizer from a blocking resource
steps.look: The resource is deleted and the namespace proceeds. Check for orphaned cloud resources afterwards.
steps.note: Skips the cleanup that the owning controller was waiting to perform. For a resource representing cloud infrastructure, that infrastructure is orphaned and keeps costing money with nothing tracking it. Identify which controller owns the finalizer and why it is stuck before removing it.

causes.cause: Resources with finalizers remain.
causes.fix: Find the owning controller. If it is gone, its finalizers will never be released and must be removed manually.

causes.cause: An aggregated API service is unavailable.
causes.fix: Fix or delete the APIService. Metrics-server and custom API servers commonly cause this.

causes.cause: An operator that owned finalizers was uninstalled.
causes.fix: Remove its finalizers. Uninstalling an operator before its resources is the usual sequence error.

causes.cause: A webhook rejects the deletion.
causes.fix: Check failurePolicy. A webhook pointing at a deleted service blocks everything.

verify: The namespace is gone.
No orphaned cloud resources remain.
The root cause was addressed rather than forced past.

title: Pods take a very long time to start pulling images
summary: Deployments crawl because image pulls dominate startup time.

steps.title: Measure how long the pull took
steps.look: The Pulled event includes the elapsed time. Anything over a minute for a normal service image is worth investigating.

signals.means: The pull is slow enough to matter.
Still pulling. Watch rather than assume it is stuck.

steps.title: Check the image size
steps.look: Then check that image's size in the registry. Multi-gigabyte images are the most common cause and the easiest to fix.

steps.title: Check the pull policy
steps.look: Always re-checks the registry every start. With a mutable tag like latest that means a full pull far more often than you expect.

steps.title: Check whether the node already has it cached
steps.look: A pod scheduled onto a fresh node always pulls cold. Autoscaled clusters pay this cost constantly.

causes.cause: The image is very large.
causes.fix: Use multi-stage builds and a slim base. This is the highest-leverage fix.

causes.cause: imagePullPolicy Always with a mutable tag.
causes.fix: Pin by digest and use IfNotPresent where the tag is immutable.

causes.cause: The registry is geographically distant.
causes.fix: Use a regional mirror or a pull-through cache.

causes.cause: New nodes have no cached layers.
causes.fix: Pre-pull critical images with a DaemonSet, or use a node image that includes them.

causes.cause: The registry is rate-limiting.
causes.fix: Authenticate, or mirror the image internally. Anonymous pulls from public registries are limited.

verify: Pull time is a few seconds on a warm node.
Rollouts complete in a reasonable window.

title: Pods will not run on a specific node pool
summary: Nodes exist and have capacity but the scheduler avoids them.

steps.title: List taints on every node
steps.look: Which nodes carry taints and with what effect. NoSchedule blocks new pods; NoExecute also evicts running ones.

signals.means: Existing pods are evicted too, not just new ones blocked.
New pods are blocked unless they tolerate the taint.

steps.title: Check the pod's tolerations
steps.look: A toleration must match the key, value and effect. Kubernetes adds default tolerations for node conditions, so ignore those.

steps.title: Check node labels against the selector
steps.look: Taints and selectors are separate mechanisms. A pod usually needs both a toleration and a matching selector to land on dedicated nodes.

steps.title: Check whether the autoscaler knows about the taint
steps.look: A cluster autoscaler will not scale up a tainted pool for a pod that does not tolerate it, so the pod stays Pending forever.

causes.cause: The pod does not tolerate the node's taint.
causes.fix: Add a toleration matching key, value and effect exactly.

causes.cause: A NoExecute taint evicts running pods.
causes.fix: Add a toleration with tolerationSeconds, or remove the taint if it was not intended.

causes.cause: The pod tolerates the taint but has no reason to prefer those nodes.
causes.fix: Tolerations permit; they do not attract. Add nodeAffinity to target the pool.

causes.cause: The toleration key or value does not match.
causes.fix: These are exact string comparisons. Compare character by character.

verify: The pod schedules onto the intended pool.
Nodes in that pool are used as expected.

title: Node drain hangs forever
summary: kubectl drain never completes because a disruption budget will not allow eviction.

steps.title: Read what drain is waiting on
steps.look: The pods it cannot evict and why. Cannot evict due to a budget is very different from a pod with local storage.

signals.means: A PodDisruptionBudget forbids the eviction.
The pod uses local storage, which drain refuses to discard without a flag.
Normal. DaemonSet pods are not drained.

steps.title: Check allowed disruptions on each budget
steps.look: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS at zero means eviction is blocked. That is the budget doing its job, not a bug.

steps.title: Check whether the workload has healthy replicas elsewhere
steps.look: If all replicas sit on this node, no eviction can satisfy the budget. That is a spread problem.

steps.title: Check for pods with no controller
steps.cmd: kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName={node} -o json | findstr ownerReferences
steps.look: A bare pod with no controller will not be recreated elsewhere, so drain refuses it without --force.

causes.cause: A disruption budget forbids eviction.
causes.fix: Scale the workload up so the budget can be satisfied, or relax minAvailable during maintenance.

causes.cause: Every replica is on this node.
causes.fix: Add pod anti-affinity or topology spread so replicas distribute.

causes.cause: Pods use emptyDir or local volumes.
causes.fix: --delete-emptydir-data discards that data. Confirm nothing important is in it.

causes.cause: A pod has no owning controller.
causes.fix: --force deletes it permanently; it will not come back. Move it to a Deployment instead.

verify: The drain completes.
Workloads are running on other nodes.
No budget was permanently weakened.

title: CronJob runs pile up or overlap
summary: Jobs accumulate, or two runs execute at once and corrupt each other.

steps.title: Count how many jobs exist
steps.look: Many completed jobs means history limits are too high. Many active jobs at once means concurrency is not restricted.

signals.means: More than one run is active simultaneously.

steps.title: Read the concurrency and history settings
steps.look: Allow is the default and permits overlap. History limits control how many finished jobs are retained.

steps.title: Check for missed schedules
steps.look: If the controller was down past startingDeadlineSeconds, runs are skipped entirely rather than queued.

steps.title: Clean up finished jobs
steps.look: The job list shrinks. Set history limits so this does not need doing by hand again.
steps.note: Deletes every successful Job in the namespace along with its pods and their logs. If anyone needs those logs for an audit trail, collect them first. Running jobs are untouched.

causes.cause: concurrencyPolicy is Allow.
causes.fix: Use Forbid for jobs that must not overlap, or Replace to cancel the previous run.

causes.cause: History limits retain too many jobs.
causes.fix: Lower successfulJobsHistoryLimit. The default of three is usually right.

causes.cause: Runs take longer than the interval.
causes.fix: Either make the job faster or widen the schedule. Overlap is a symptom.

causes.cause: startingDeadlineSeconds expired.
causes.fix: Raise it, or accept that runs are skipped when the controller is unavailable.

verify: One run active at a time.
Job history stays bounded.
No schedule is silently missed.

title: Application cannot authenticate to the API server
summary: In-cluster code gets 401 or cannot find its ServiceAccount token.

steps.title: Check the ServiceAccount on the pod
steps.look: Empty means the default ServiceAccount, which typically has almost no permissions. That is the usual cause of an in-cluster 401.

signals.means: Using the default ServiceAccount, which has no meaningful RBAC.

steps.title: Check the token is mounted
steps.look: token, ca.crt and namespace should be present. Absent means automountServiceAccountToken is false somewhere.

signals.means: No token is mounted at all.

steps.title: Check automount settings
steps.look: This can be disabled on the ServiceAccount or on the pod. The pod setting wins.

steps.title: Check what that identity is allowed to do
steps.look: The effective permissions for that ServiceAccount. Comparing against what the app needs usually makes the gap obvious.

causes.cause: Using the default ServiceAccount.
causes.fix: Create a dedicated one and bind only the permissions the app needs.

causes.cause: Token automounting is disabled.
causes.fix: Enable it on the pod if the app genuinely needs API access.

causes.cause: The ServiceAccount has no binding.
causes.fix: Create a Role and RoleBinding. Grant the narrowest set that works.

causes.cause: A legacy long-lived token expired.
causes.fix: Modern tokens are projected and rotate automatically. Use the projected volume rather than a Secret.

causes.cause: The binding is in a different namespace.
causes.fix: RoleBindings are namespaced. The binding must be where the resource lives.

verify: The application authenticates.
It has only the permissions it needs.
The token rotates rather than being a static Secret.

title: Container cannot write to its filesystem
summary: The app fails on writes even though it worked before hardening was applied.

steps.title: Check the security context
steps.look: readOnlyRootFilesystem true means every write outside a mounted volume fails by design.

signals.means: The root filesystem is read-only on purpose.
Running as a specific UID. It may not own the paths it needs.

steps.title: Find where it is trying to write
steps.look: The path in the error. Temp directories and cache paths are the usual ones applications forget about.

steps.title: Check what volumes are mounted
steps.look: Whether a writable volume covers the path it needs. An emptyDir at that path is usually the whole fix.

steps.title: Check volume ownership settings
steps.look: fsGroup chowns mounted volumes to that group on mount. Without it, a non-root user often cannot write to a fresh volume.

causes.cause: The root filesystem is read-only.
causes.fix: Mount an emptyDir at the path that needs writes. Keep the rootfs read-only; it is a good default.

causes.cause: The container user does not own the path.
causes.fix: Set fsGroup so volumes are chowned on mount.

causes.cause: The app writes to /tmp with a read-only rootfs.
causes.fix: Mount an emptyDir at /tmp. Almost every hardened workload needs this.

causes.cause: A hostPath mount has restrictive ownership.
causes.fix: Fix ownership on the host, or use a proper volume type.

verify: The application writes successfully.
The root filesystem stays read-only.
Writable paths are explicit volumes.
escalate: Which path the write failed on

title: NodePort service is not reachable from outside
summary: The Service exists with a node port but connections from outside the cluster time out.

steps.title: Confirm the allocated node port
steps.look: The type must be NodePort or LoadBalancer. The port is in the 30000 to 32767 range unless configured otherwise.

signals.means: ClusterIP is internal only. There is no node port to reach.

steps.title: Check the Service has endpoints
steps.look: No endpoints means the node port answers with nothing. Fix that before looking at the network.

steps.title: Test from a node itself
steps.look: Get a node IP, then curl that IP on the node port from somewhere inside the network. Working there but not from outside isolates it to the firewall.

steps.title: Check externalTrafficPolicy
steps.look: Local means only nodes actually running a pod will answer. Hitting any other node gives a timeout that looks like a firewall problem.

causes.cause: The Service is ClusterIP.
causes.fix: Change the type to NodePort or LoadBalancer.

causes.cause: The node port is blocked at the cloud firewall.
causes.fix: Open the port range in the security group. It is closed by default.

causes.cause: externalTrafficPolicy is Local.
causes.fix: Only nodes with a pod respond. Use Cluster, or target nodes that host the workload.

causes.cause: The Service has no ready endpoints.
causes.fix: Follow the no-endpoints runbook.

causes.cause: Using an internal IP from outside the network.
causes.fix: Use the external address, or a load balancer in front.

verify: The service answers on the node port from outside.
It answers from any node, or Local is understood.
escalate: Whether it works from inside the network

title: Commands run against the wrong cluster
summary: You applied something and it landed in the wrong environment.

steps.title: Show the active context and its cluster
steps.cmd: kubectl config current-context && kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}'
steps.look: The server URL, not just the context name. Names lie; the URL does not.

steps.title: List every context available
steps.look: The asterisk marks the active one. Similar names between environments are how accidents happen.

steps.title: Check the default namespace for this context
steps.look: An empty value means default. Commands without -n go there, which is rarely what you want in a shared cluster.

steps.title: Switch deliberately before doing anything
steps.look: current-context shows the intended cluster. Confirm the server URL again.
steps.note: Changes which cluster every subsequent kubectl command talks to, for every shell on this machine. If another terminal is mid-task it will silently switch too. Prefer --context on individual commands when working across clusters at the same time.

causes.cause: Context names look alike.
causes.fix: Rename them to be unmistakable. Put the environment first.

causes.cause: Nothing shows the active context.
causes.fix: Add it to your shell prompt. This single change prevents most of these incidents.

causes.cause: The context has no namespace set.
causes.fix: Set one per context so bare commands land somewhere predictable.

causes.cause: One kubeconfig for every cluster.
causes.fix: Use --context explicitly, or separate files with KUBECONFIG.

causes.cause: You already applied to the wrong cluster.
causes.fix: Check what changed before reverting. A blind delete can make it worse.

verify: The context matches the intended environment.
The prompt shows it.
A guardrail exists for production.

title: Replica count oscillates up and down
summary: The autoscaler scales up then straight back down, churning pods continuously.

steps.title: Watch the replica count over time
steps.look: How often REPLICAS changes. Several changes a minute is flapping; a change every few minutes is normal response.

signals.means: Read the current, min and max. A target close to the actual utilisation makes small swings trigger scaling.

steps.title: Read the scaling behaviour policy
steps.look: Empty means defaults. The default scale-down stabilisation is five minutes, so flapping faster than that means something overrides it.

steps.title: Check whether new pods distort the metric
steps.look: A pod still warming up reports high CPU, which triggers more scaling, which adds more warming pods. That is the feedback loop.

causes.cause: The target utilisation sits right at normal load.
causes.fix: Lower the target so ordinary variation does not cross it.

causes.cause: Scale-down stabilisation is too short.
causes.fix: Raise behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds.

causes.cause: New pods report high usage while starting.
causes.fix: Add a startup allowance, or scale on a metric that excludes warmup.

causes.cause: The load itself is spiky.
causes.fix: Scale on a smoothed metric such as queue depth rather than instantaneous CPU.

verify: Replica count settles and changes only with real load trends.
Pod churn stops.
escalate: Whether new pods distort the metric

title: Every create fails with a webhook error
summary: Admission webhooks reject or time out, so nothing can be applied.

steps.title: Read the admission error
steps.look: The webhook name is in the message. That tells you which controller to look at.

signals.means: The webhook did not answer in time.
The API server does not trust the webhook's certificate.
The webhook answered and refused. This is policy working.

steps.title: Check the webhook's backing service
steps.look: Which configurations exist and what service each points at. A webhook pointing at a deleted service blocks everything it matches.

steps.title: Check the webhook pods are running
steps.cmd: kubectl get pods -A | findstr /I "webhook admission policy"
steps.look: The controller must be running and ready. A crashed policy engine takes the cluster's write path with it.

steps.title: Check the failure policy
steps.look: Fail means an unreachable webhook blocks everything. Ignore means it is skipped. That single setting decides whether an outage is total.

causes.cause: The webhook is slow or unreachable.
causes.fix: Fix the controller. Consider a namespaceSelector so kube-system is exempt.

causes.cause: The certificate is untrusted or expired.
causes.fix: Rotate the caBundle. Cert-manager-issued webhook certs expire like any other.

causes.cause: A policy genuinely rejected the resource.
causes.fix: Read the message and fix the manifest. This is the system working.

causes.cause: The backing service was deleted.
causes.fix: Delete the webhook configuration too, or restore the service.

causes.cause: failurePolicy is Fail with no exemptions.
causes.fix: Exempt kube-system so a broken webhook cannot lock you out entirely.

verify: Resources apply successfully.
The webhook controller is healthy.
System namespaces are exempt.
escalate: Whether the backing pods are ready

title: kubectl top does not work
summary: Resource metrics are unavailable, which also breaks autoscaling.

steps.title: Read the error from top
steps.look: Whether the API is absent or present but failing. Those are different problems.

signals.means: The API service is not registered or not ready.

signals.match: error: You must be logged in
signals.means: An authentication problem rather than a metrics one.

steps.title: Check the API service is available
steps.look: AVAILABLE must be True. False carries a reason, usually that the service endpoint is unreachable.

steps.title: Check the metrics-server pod
steps.look: Running and ready. CrashLooping is usually a TLS problem talking to kubelets.

steps.title: Read its logs
steps.look: Certificate errors against the kubelet are the most common failure on self-managed clusters.

causes.cause: metrics-server is not installed.
causes.fix: Install it. It is not part of a base cluster.

causes.cause: The API service cannot reach the pod.
causes.fix: Check the service and any NetworkPolicy in kube-system.

causes.cause: metrics-server cannot verify kubelet certificates.
causes.fix: Configure it properly, or use --kubelet-insecure-tls only in a lab.

causes.cause: Your credentials are the problem, not metrics.
causes.fix: Follow the API access runbook.

verify: kubectl top returns figures.
The API service reports available.
HPAs show real targets.

title: Pod rejected by Pod Security admission
summary: Creating a pod fails because it violates the namespace's security level.

steps.title: Read the violation message
steps.look: It lists every field that violates the policy. Each one must be fixed; there is no partial pass.

signals.means: Must be set to false explicitly.
The pod must declare it runs as non-root.
A seccomp profile must be specified.
Host access is forbidden at this level.

steps.title: Check the namespace's enforced level
steps.look: The pod-security labels. baseline is permissive; restricted requires a full security context on every container.

steps.title: Check what the pod declares
steps.look: Compare against the requirements. Under restricted, omitting a field is a violation rather than a default.

causes.cause: allowPrivilegeEscalation is not false.
causes.fix: Set it explicitly. Omitting it fails under restricted.

causes.cause: The pod does not declare runAsNonRoot.
causes.fix: Set runAsNonRoot true and give a numeric runAsUser. The image must support it.

causes.cause: No seccomp profile.
causes.fix: Set seccompProfile type RuntimeDefault.

causes.cause: The pod requests host namespaces or paths.
causes.fix: Not permitted at baseline or above. Redesign, or run it in a dedicated namespace with a lower level.

causes.cause: The namespace level is stricter than intended.
causes.fix: Adjust the label deliberately, with a reason recorded.

verify: The pod is admitted.
It runs as non-root with a full security context.
The namespace level was not weakened casually.

title: Node reports DiskPressure
summary: The kubelet is evicting pods because the node is low on disk.

steps.title: Confirm the condition
steps.look: True with a message naming which resource. nodefs and imagefs are separate thresholds with separate causes.

signals.means: Image storage is full. Garbage collection is not keeping up.
The node's own filesystem is full, usually logs or ephemeral storage.

steps.title: See what pods were evicted
steps.look: Evicted pods with their reason. Best-effort pods go first, which tells you who was not declaring requests.

steps.title: Check image garbage collection thresholds
